title: A Shropshire Lad II: date and occasion
short: Untitled poem II of A Shropshire Lad (1896); first drafted in spring 1895, with the middle stanza added and rewritten later.
body: Housman's sequence A Shropshire Lad (1896) numbers its poems rather than titling them; this is II, known by its first line. The surviving draft has been dated to April or May 1895 and had only two stanzas; the arithmetic middle stanza was composed later and much revised. Burnett's edition notes that the cherry was personal: there was a locally admired cherry tree at Housman's childhood home, he recorded the cherries' flowering in his diary in the 1890s, and in later life he planted cherry trees at Trinity College, Cambridge. The poem is among the most anthologised of English lyrics.

anchor: hung with bloom along the bough
title: Metre and rhyme
short: Rhymed couplets of iambic tetrameter; the three-syllable 'Loveliest' at the very start unsettles the metre to striking effect.
body: The poem is in three quatrains made of rhyming couplets (now/bough, ride/Eastertide), in four-stress iambic lines, many of them headless (seven syllables). The Housman Society notes that the first word, 'Loveliest', disrupts the metre: its three syllables crowd the opening foot, so the poem begins with an overflow of feeling before settling into regularity. The simple metre, close to hymn and ballad, is typical of A Shropshire Lad and belies the arithmetic precision of the argument. 'Is hung with bloom' anticipates the poem's last line, 'hung with snow', binding beginning to end.

title: ride
short: A 'ride' is a broad track through a wood, wide enough to ride a horse along.
body: In this sense 'ride' is a noun for a path or green road cut through woodland, used especially for riding or hunting; the OED records it from the eighteenth century. The Housman Society glosses it as a path broad enough for a horse. The cherry 'stands about' the ride, lining it, as if the trees were spectators at a procession, and the next line dresses them for a festival.

title: Wearing white for Eastertide
short: White is the church's colour for Easter; the blossoming tree is dressed for the feast of resurrection, though the poem offers none.
body: Eastertide is the season of Easter. White is the liturgical colour of the feast, and in the early church the newly baptised wore white robes through Easter week, so the tree is personified as a celebrant in festal dress. The religious allusion is pointed: the season celebrates resurrection and eternal life, while the poem goes on to count a single, limited life in years. Burnett lists among possible analogues Robert Bridges' 'Spring goeth all in white', which shares the image of spring dressed in white. The cherry's whiteness also prepares the final transformation into 'snow'.

title: threescore years and ten
short: The Bible's span of a human life, seventy years (Psalm 90:10), which the speaker uses as his reckoning.
body: The phrase comes from Psalm 90:10 in the King James Bible and the Prayer Book: 'The days of our years are threescore years and ten'. The psalm is a meditation on the brevity of life before an eternal God and is read at the Anglican burial service, so it brings a funereal undertone into a spring poem. Housman, an atheist by the time he wrote the poem, borrows the measure without the consolation. The speaker accepts the biblical allotment as a fact and then does sums with it.

title: Twenty will not come again
short: The speaker is twenty; the persona is young, though Housman was in his mid-thirties when he wrote the poem.
body: The speaker has lived twenty years, which 'will not come again', and so has 'fifty more' springs. The arithmetic is deliberately plain, almost comic, in the manner of a country lad. The speaker is a persona: Housman himself was about thirty-six in 1895. Critics have read the poem as a young man's first recognition of his own mortality, prompted by the short-lived cherry blossom (Leggett, Firchow, as summarised in the Wikipedia article). The phrase 'will not come again' looks ahead to 'And cannot come again' at the end of A Shropshire Lad XL, one of the sequence's recurrent laments for lost time.

title: Fifty springs are little room
short: Fifty springs seem too few to see enough blossom: a carpe diem paradox in which a long life feels short.
body: The paradox of the last stanza is that half a century is 'little room' (too little space) for looking at things in bloom. The poem therefore resolves not in pleasure-seeking but in looking: 'I will go / To see'. D. T. Siebert called it 'a little masterpiece of carpe diem' (as quoted in the Wikipedia summary); other critics stress its sense that beauty is precious because it is brief. Peter Firchow, by contrast, judged the middle stanza convoluted, so critical opinion is not unanimous. The phrase 'little room' may recall Marlowe's 'infinite riches in a little room' (The Jew of Malta), one of the analogues Burnett lists.

title: hung with snow
short: The blossom seen as snow: a lovely image of white flowers that also brings winter, age and death into the spring.
body: The poem ends by transforming the cherry's 'bloom' of l. 2 into 'snow'. On one level the image simply describes masses of white blossom. But snow belongs to winter, and to the old age and death that the arithmetic has just measured, so the last word quietly carries the end of the reckoning into the moment of beauty. It may also hint that the speaker will go on looking even into winter, when the boughs are hung with real snow. The ambiguity between celebration and memento mori is the source of the poem's tension; the plain diction hides it.

anchor: About the woodlands I will go
title: Reception and musical settings
short: One of the most set of English poems: over sixty composers, including Butterworth, Somervell, Gurney and Moeran, have set it.
body: The poem's song-like regularity made it a favourite of English composers. More than sixty settings are known, among them George Butterworth's Six Songs from A Shropshire Lad (1911) and his orchestral rhapsody, Arthur Somervell's song cycle, and settings by Ivor Gurney, E. J. Moeran and C. W. Orr. Many of these composers wrote in the years around the First World War, when the sequence's dead young men took on new meaning; Butterworth himself was killed on the Somme in 1916. In a 1995 BBC poll the poem was among the nation's hundred favourites.
